Role: Product designer (product strategy, interaction design, UI Kit, front-end MVP build) Type : Case Study | Timeline: October 2026 Built with: Figma → React, Vite, Tailwind, Phosphor icons Live build: https://presm.netlify.app/ Press enter or click to view image in full size Banner image L ike most designers, I collect things. Doesnt matter if its related to design or biking or anything else. They show up in my feed, I think “I’ll need that someday, it’s interesting” and I save them. As long as its something interesting, it’ll go in my bookmarks. For a while I saved them in a long Markdown file called raj-finds.md . In a couple of days days it grew to 67 entries in six batches, covering computer vision, hardware, AI agents, generative art, UI kits and more. Then I needed one of them to share with a fellow designer friend, and I couldn't find it. The link was in the file. I'd just forgotten what the thing was called, and the bookmark didn't say why I'd cared about it. All I had was a title and a URL. That’s the problem this project is about. The real problem: “I need a better bookmark manager” sounds like the problem, but it isn’t. There are plenty of bookmark managers, and they all fail in the same way. For me atleast. So I wrote down what actually goes wrong when I go back to a saved link: 1. The link survives. The reason doesn’t. When I save something, I know exactly why it’s interesting. Three weeks later I don’t. A bookmark keeps a URL and drops the reasoning, which was the valuable part. 2. Things belong in more than one place. An AI agent memory tool belongs in “Agent tooling” and in “Read this week.” Folders make you pick one. People end up with duplicates, or they stop filing at all. 3. I remember what it does, not what it’s called. I remember “the one that tracks points through video even when they’re hidden.” I don’t remember “TapNet.” Search that only matches names misses how memory actually works. So the problem statement became: How might we help one person save the things they find in a way that still makes sense to them months later? Note the word later . The tool isn’t for the moment of saving. It’s for my future self, who has somehow lost all the context. A bookmark should be a small judgement: Press enter or click to view image in full size Answering the What, Why, Who Before screens, I wrote five questions. Every link in my Markdown file had to answer them: What is it for? One sentence, specific. Not “web framework.” Why this one? What makes it different. Who is it for? One person: “If you’re building X…” What’s the tradeoff? What it’s honestly not good for. One concrete example of someone using it. I went back through all 67 entries and answered them. Yeah it was painful. And it was slow. But it changed how I treated the list. The file changed from being a pile of links and started reading like a set of recommendations. That someone was me, a few days earlier. The fourth question did the most work. Recording what a resource is not suitable for is what makes a saved link something you can act on. “TapNet is research code in notebooks, not a polished product” saves me an afternoon. “PLFM Radar needs serious RF skills and has regulatory implications” stops me before I order parts. So the design principle behind the whole product is: Saving should take a bit of effort, because that effort is what makes finding things easy. It goes against the usual “make capture effortless” advice, and I chose that on purpose. Capture tools that cost nothing produce piles of links nobody reads. I’d rather have 67 entries I trust than 600 I skim past. Who I designed for: Press enter or click to view image in full size For the User. By the User. I designed and built it for me. I treated my own failures as data. Using the tool myself showed me two possible different modes, so I designed for both: The curator. Writes the entries, cares about quality, and adds, edits and removes resources. In the app this is the Admin role. The reader. Browses, searches, saves things into their own collections and shares links. They use the library without changing it. This is the Reader role. Most of the time these are the same person on different days. Splitting them made something clear: the library and your collections are separate things. The library is curated and shared. Your collections are personal. That separation runs through the whole data model. Design decisions (and why) 1. The form asks the five questions in plain language Press enter or click to view image in full size The capture form The upload form is the differentiator here. Every field has a label phrased as a question and a hint that pushes back a little: What is this repo? One sentence, specific. Not “web framework”. Why this repo?
